desc:
For a string s of length n, build the array pi of length n where pi[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of s[0..i] that is also a suffix of s[0..i]. A proper prefix is shorter than the whole substring, so pi[0] is always 0.

Example: for s = "aabaaab" the answer is [0,1,0,1,2,2,3]. For the last prefix "aabaaab" the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix is "aab", which has length 3.

Return the array. A solution that runs in O(n) time exists (this array is the heart of the KMP algorithm).
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Computing every pi[i] by comparing all candidate lengths is O(n2) or worse. Look for a relation between pi[i] and pi[i-1].
If the prefix of length k = pi[i-1] can be extended, that is s[k] == s[i], then pi[i] = k + 1.
If s[k] != s[i], the next best candidate border of s[0..i-1] is the border of the border, k = pi[k-1]. Repeat until the characters agree or k is zero.
editorial: Process the string left to right and keep k, the length of the longest border of the previous prefix. Every border of s[0..i] that has length at least 1 is a border of s[0..i-1] extended by the character s[i]. So we look through the borders of s[0..i-1] from the longest to the shortest, and take the first one that is followed by the character s[i].
The borders of a prefix form a chain: after the longest border of length k, the next longest is pi[k-1], then pi[pi[k-1]-1] and so on. This is why a mismatch is handled by k = pi[k-1].

Amortised analysis: k grows by at most one per character and every fallback step strictly decreases it, never below zero. The total number of fallback steps is therefore at most n, giving O(n) time and O(n) space for the output.
